# Dynamics of the Global Digital Divide during the COVID-19 Pandemic

- SPATIAL FEATURES OF SECTORAL DEVELOPMENT
- Open access
- Published: 27 November 2025

- A. V. Nagirnaya 1 

### Abstract

In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, the need of the population and the economy to use digital technologies has increased unprecedentedly. The level of digitalization has become one of the key factors for sustainability and adaptation to new conditions. Have these changes led to shifts in the geography of the Internet and a narrowing of the global digital divide? The article is devoted to identifying the features, trends and quantitative parameters of the dynamics of digital inequality during the pandemic in order to confirm or refute the hypothesis of a reduction in the global three-level digital divide in 2019–2023. The three-level digital divide model was used as a theoretical basis. The set of research methods included statistical calculations, graphical interpretation of data, comparative geographical approach, logical analysis, and case studies. The data comprised official statistics from international and scientific and educational organizations and analytical materials from consulting and other companies specializing in Internet development issues. The hypothesis about the reduction of the intercountry gap in the area of technical and price availability of high-quality Internet (the first level of digital inequality), as well as in the area of online orders for goods/services (the third level) was confirmed. The hypothesis about the reduction of the second-level gap associated with various aspects of social inequality has been refuted. The analysis showed that as digital services develop and become more complex, the digital divide is increasingly governed not so much by the availability of the Internet, but by the ability and skill to use it effectively. In terms of the number of Internet users per 100 inhabitants, the gap between countries is fourfold, and in terms of the share of the population using the Internet to order goods and services, it is an order of magnitude higher (38-fold). Quantitative disparities are narrowing faster than qualitative gaps related to gender, age, commercial use of the Internet and the distribution of its information resources.

## INTRODUCTION AND FORMULATION OF THE PROBLEM

The Internet is a key innovation of our time, on the basis of which, as a result of the convergence of information and communication technologies (ICT), an integrated system of global digital communications has been created (Nagirnaya 2013; Sintserov 2005). The rapid expansion of the Internet, simultaneously with the spread of mobile communications, the penetration of digital technologies into all spheres of public life, and the transition to a digital economy, is usually called digitalization (Abroskin et al., 2019). The development of the Internet and digitalization are today the driving force behind the socio-economic development of countries and regions and an important factor in economic growth (Ponomareva, 2021; Zemtsov et al., 2022).

The spread of ICT occurs unevenly spatially and is subject to the laws of diffusion of innovations (Nagirnaya, 2014; Perfil’ev, 2003; Yu, 2011; Zemtsov and Baburin, 2017). The life cycle of any innovation has the form of a wave and consists of several stages: origin, diffusion, accumulation and saturation (Hagerstrand, 1967). Different countries are at different stages of diffusion of a particular innovation, as are different regions within a single country. There are three diffusion models: area (or neighborhood), hierarchical (cascade) and network (chain). Whereas the expansion of the Internet took place in the world according to the principle of hierarchical distribution from the largest cities to smaller ones, from the countries of the center to the countries of the semiperiphery and periphery, the spread of cellular communications proceeded according to the principle of chain diffusion: without reaching saturation in developed countries, the wave of the spread of mobile telephony covered developing countries, which rapidly overtook developed countries in terms of the level of mobile telephony (Nagirnaya, 2013).

The level of digitalization of a particular territory is determined by a number of factors: the well-being of the population, the development of basic telecommunications infrastructure, the average age and level of education of the population, the favorability of the institutional and economic environment for the development of the ICT sector, as well as geographical factors. The latter include: informational and geographical position with respect to sources of innovation (manifestation of neighborhood diffusion) and major telecommunications highways, level of urbanization and size of the central city (manifestation of hierarchical diffusion), landscape, size of the territory (Nagirnaya, 2013; Zemtsov et al., 2022), as well as the political situation (presence/absence of military conflicts).

The problem of territorial disproportions in the development of digitalization processes has become one of the most pressing in the first quarter of the 21st century, and its study provides a starting point for understanding the essence of the social landscape of the 21st century (Gainanov and Sharifyanov, 2014; Maksakovsky, 2010; Robinson et al., 2015; The Global …, 2021; Van Dijk, 2012). The digital divide concept was formulated in the late 1990s (Castells, 1996), and it was first officially declared in 2000 in the Okinawa Charter of the Global Information Society (Okinawa Charter, 2000). The terms digital divide and digital inequality are considered synonyms by most researchers (Kostyaev, 2024).

The threat of the digital divide is that representatives of information-poor regions or social groups will find themselves in a “different Universe” in terms of opportunities for inclusion in the global information society (Korovkin et al., 2020). Some authors call this phenomenon the digitalization paradox: regions that can potentially benefit the most from digitalization and need it the most (e.g., remote or rural) are the least connected (Salemink et al., 2017). Thus, digital inequality creates the preconditions for further strengthening of socioeconomic differentiation and polarization, exacerbating the existing unevenness of spatial development (Haefner and Sternberg, 2020).

Initially, digital inequality was considered only from a technical point of view as a growing lag of some countries, regions, and social groups with respect to others in access to modern digital technologies, but very soon the scientific community realized that this is a multi-faceted phenomenon that develops over time. In 2001, a theory of two types of digital inequality appeared: the first characterizes the inequality of access to the Internet infrastructure, and the second, disproportions in the possibilities of its use (Hargittai, 2001), associated with differences in income (Polozhikhina, 2017), education level (Avila, 2009; Shinyaeva and Slepova, 2019), age (Gruzdeva, 2022; Israelashvili and Kim, 2012), gender (Davaki, 2018), etc. Later, some authors began to talk about the motivational/psychological aspect of digital inequality and even highlight it as a separate level (Gainanov and Sharifyanov, 2014; Van Dijk, 2012). However, most modern researchers agree on a three-level model, according to which the following levels of digital inequality are distinguished: (1) infrastructural, (2) social, and (3) economic. Most scientific publications study one level (Gruzdeva, 2022; Kapelyuk and Karelin, 2023; Kostyaev, 2024; etc.

The literature describes three stages of the global spread of the Internet: early (before 2000), expansion (2001–2010), and mature (2011–2019) (Nagirnaya, 2013, 2018). This article analyzes the five-year period that covered the years of the COVID-19 pandemic, the end of which was declared by the WHO in May 2023. During the pandemic, the need for the population and economy to use digital technologies has increased to an unprecedented level. For the first time, the Internet has become not only a means of communication, self-realization, doing business, and obtaining information, but also the most important condition for physical, economic, and psychoemotional survival (Starikova and Demidova, 2021). The level of digitalization has become one of the key factors of sustainability and adaptation to the consequences of global changes (Zemtsov et al., 2022). Has this led to shifts in the geography of the Internet and a narrowing of the global digital divide (DD) at all levels? This is the research question that the author poses to himself.

The purpose of this study is to identify the features, trends and quantitative parameters of the dynamics of digital inequality during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study aims to confirm or refute the hypothesis that the global three-level digital divide has narrowed during the specified period. Based on this goal, by analyzing the dynamics of indicators for 2019–2023, the following problems were formulated and solved: (1) identifying the dynamics of the first level of DD indicators and shifts in the geography of the Internet for the specified period (in the area of Internet penetration, the gap between city and village, in connection speed and affordability); (2) determining the dynamics of various aspects of the second level of the DD, namely, gender disparities, digital literacy of the population, disparities in the information content of the Internet; (3) identifying shifts in global Internet trade and the population’s use of the Internet order goods and services; (4) characteristics of Russia’s place in the global dynamics of the DD.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

The methodological tools of the research are based on a three-level model of digital inequality, which has become widely used in foreign and domestic studies (Blanutsa, 2024; Gainanov and Sharifyanov, 2014; Gruzdeva 2020; Lai and Widmar, 2021; Nieminen, 2016; Ragnedda, 2017; Safiullin and Moiseeva, 2019; Sassi, 2005; Zemtsov et al., 2022; Yu, 2011). We agree with the positions of contemporary authors and base our research on the following three levels of the DD:

(1) the basic level of the DD—infrastructure—includes such aspects as the quantitative gap in access to the Internet, including between the city and the village, as well as disparities in the affordability of the Internet and access speed. The study analyzes several access options: wired/fixed (dedicated line) and wireless (mobile, satellite) with a special focus on broadband, which form the framework of the Internet infrastructure;

(2) the second-level of the DD is caused by various aspects of social inequality and includes social disparities in the intensity of Internet use, caused by barriers in the areas of digital literacy, gender, age, language inequality, etc.;

(3) the third level of the DD denotes the use of the Internet for commercial purposes (e-commerce, Internet banking, etc.).

The set of research methods includes statistical analysis, graphical interpretation of data, comparative geographical approach, logical analysis, case study, etc. The study is based on official statistics from international organizations (ITU, OECD, Eurostat, World Bank, UNCTAD, etc.); the Institute for Statistical Studies and Economics of Knowledge of the HSE University; the Internet resource Domains of Russia and the CENTR association; and analytical materials from consulting and other companies examining Internet development trends in Russia and the world. The use of official statistical data as the main source generally ensures stable reproducibility of calculations, openness, objectivity and comparability of assessment results, while, as a rule, requiring additional research
